title: Consecutive and modal connectors
schema: english-prompt -> learner types German -> Reveal/Hide answer shows reference + speaker

exercises.english: The train was late, so we missed the bus.
exercises.german: Der Zug hatte Verspätung, deshalb verpassten wir den Bus.
exercises.why: deshalb in position I simply links two independent main clauses without a conjunction, and the main-clause verb keeps its position II form verpassten.

exercises.english: The window is broken, so I will close the door instead.
exercises.german: Das Fenster ist kaputt, daher mache ich stattdessen die Tür zu.
exercises.why: daher signals a consequence that follows logically from the broken window, and stattdessen contrasts the substituted action.

exercises.english: She studied a lot, so she passed the exam with distinction.
exercises.german: Sie hat viel gelernt, also bestand sie die Prüfung mit Auszeichnung.
exercises.why: Die Bahnverbindung also closes the two main clauses formally; the perfect tense of the first clause and the simple past of the second are normal narrative.

exercises.english: It is very cold outside, so the radiator is switched on again.
exercises.german: Es ist draußen sehr kalt, deshalb wird die Heizung wieder eingeschaltet.
exercises.why: With a passive main clause, the conjugated form of werden sits in position II while the participle einschaltet closes the clause.

exercises.english: The meeting has been moved, so the team cannot attend today.
exercises.german: Die Besprechung wurde verschoben, daher kann das Team heute nicht teilnehmen.
exercises.why: Two passive-ish statements are chained: the modal verb kann sits in position II after daher and the verb stem nehmen goes to the end of the clause.

exercises.english: The battery is empty, so I cannot take photos.
exercises.german: Der Akku ist leer, also kann ich keine Fotos machen.
exercises.why: A modal verb in position II after also makes the consequence read as a consequence of the empty battery, not as a new fact.

exercises.english: There is no paper left, so I will write it on the board.
exercises.german: Es ist kein Papier mehr da, deshalb schreibe ich es an die Tafel.
exercises.why: The pronoun es in the main clause is the subject, and deshalb pushes schreibe to position II while es moves behind the connective.

exercises.english: My colleague is ill, so I will present the results.
exercises.german: Meine Kollegin ist krank, daher stelle ich die Ergebnisse vor.
exercises.why: vorstellen separates in this sentence, and with therefore the separable prefix vor- and the verb stem stell- bracket the second position.

exercises.english: The software update failed, so nothing has changed.
exercises.german: Das Softwareupdate ist fehlgeschlagen, also hat sich nichts geändert.
exercises.why: Perfect with haben and an accusative object: hat sits in position II, geändert closes the main clause.

exercises.english: Nobody answered the phone, so I sent an email.
exercises.german: Niemand hat ans Telefon gegangen, deshalb habe ich eine E-Mail geschickt.
exercises.why: Two perfect clauses in sequence: each has its own position-II auxiliary (hat, habe) and the past participle ends the clause.

exercises.english: The hotel was fully booked, so we slept at a friend's place.
exercises.german: Das Hotel war ausgebucht, daher haben wir bei einer Freundin geschlafen.
exercises.why: haben as the position-II auxiliary of the perfect, and the preposition bei takes a dative object with a feminine noun.

exercises.english: You forgot your umbrella, so your shirt is soaked.
exercises.german: Du hast deinen Schirm vergessen, also ist dein Hemd durchnässt.
exercises.why: Vergessen is the participle of a perfect with haben, and the copula ist in position II introduces the adjective predicate durchnässt.

exercises.english: The road is blocked, so we have to take a detour.
exercises.german: Die Straße ist gesperrt, deswegen müssen wir einen Umweg fahren.
exercises.why: The modal müssen in position II expresses the forced consequence, and einen Umweg is the accusative object of the separable fahren.

exercises.english: The receipt has not arrived, so I cannot claim the expenses.
exercises.german: Die Rechnung ist noch nicht gekommen, deshalb kann ich die Spesen nicht abrechnen.
exercises.why: Two modal-present clauses: kann sits in position II and the verb stem rechnen moves to the end after the object.

exercises.english: The signal is very weak, so the connection keeps dropping.
exercises.german: Der Empfang ist sehr schwach, also bricht die Verbindung ständig ab.
exercises.why: A separable verb after a consequence adverb: abbricht is split, the prefix ab- closes the clause after the subject.

exercises.english: Nobody answered the door, so I left my name on the list.
exercises.german: Niemand hat an der Tür aufgemacht, deshalb habe ich meinen Namen auf die Liste geschrieben.
exercises.why: an der Tür is a prepositional object with the article standing in the dative; the position-II auxiliary habe carries the perfect.

exercises.english: The train leaves early tomorrow, so we should set an alarm.
exercises.german: Der Zug fährt morgen früh ab, also sollten wir einen Wecker stellen.
exercises.why: The modal sollten in position II states the necessary consequence, and abfahren is split into ab and fährt.

exercises.english: Prices have gone up again, so the trip costs more than planned.
exercises.german: Die Preise sind wieder gestiegen, daher kostet die Reise mehr als geplant.
exercises.why: Two present clauses with different subjects; the adjective predicate kostet stands in position II after daher.

exercises.english: The kettle is broken, so we drink coffee from the machine.
exercises.german: Der Wasserkocher ist kaputt, deswegen trinken wir Kaffee aus dem Automaten.
exercises.why: The preposition aus takes a dative object here, and the position-II verb trinken follows the subject wir.

exercises.english: The children were hungry after the excursion, so we stopped at a bakery.
exercises.german: Die Kinder hatten nach dem Ausflug Hunger, also sind wir bei einer Bäckerei stehen geblieben.
exercises.why: The separable verb stehen bleiben forms a past participle that is placed as a block at the end of the main clause.

exercises.english: He is so tired that he can hardly stay awake.
exercises.german: Er ist so müde, er kann kaum wach bleiben.
exercises.why: Without a that-clause, so intensifies the degree directly: the main clause reaches the limit in its own way, kann is in position II and the infinitive closes the clause.

exercises.english: The dog is so obedient that it never barks now.
exercises.german: Der Hund ist so brav, er bellt überhaupt nicht mehr.
exercises.why: Two main clauses: the degree stands in the first one and the consequence in the second, with bellt in position II.

exercises.english: The water is so clear that we can see the bottom.
exercises.german: Das Wasser ist so klar, wir sehen den Grund bis hinunter.
exercises.why: so modifies the degree of klar, and the result is expressed in the following main clause, where sehen sits in position II.

exercises.english: She talks so quickly that nobody understands her.
exercises.german: Sie redet so schnell, niemand versteht sie.
exercises.why: The degree adverb so schnell in the first main clause is answered by the negative result clause, with versteht in position II.

exercises.english: The book is so interesting that I could not put it down.
exercises.german: Das Buch ist so spannend, ich habe es nicht aus der Hand gelassen.
exercises.why: The degree of spannend is stated first, the result follows in a perfect clause whose auxiliary hat occupies position II.

exercises.english: It is so hot here that nobody can concentrate.
exercises.german: Es ist hier so heiß, keiner kann sich konzentrieren.
exercises.why: The impersonal es stands in position I, and in the second main clause the personal subject keiner comes after the connective.

exercises.english: The trail was so steep that we had to rest often.
exercises.german: Der Weg war so steil, wir mussten oft Pause machen.
exercises.why: A modal in position II with the position-II verb müssen, and the separable verb makes a block Pause machen at the end.

exercises.english: She is so honest that everyone trusts her.
exercises.german: Sie ist so ehrlich, ihr vertraut jeder.
exercises.why: so plus adjective intensifies ehrlich, and the result clause uses a pronoun object with the verb vertraut in position II.

exercises.english: The music was so loud that we could only talk by shouting.
exercises.german: Die Musik war so laut, wir konnten nur schreien.
exercises.why: A modal verb in position II expresses the limited possibility, and a verb-less second clause could not carry the result.

exercises.english: His room is so messy that no one can find anything.
exercises.german: Sein Zimmer ist so unordentlich, dort findet niemand etwas.
exercises.why: The second main clause uses a directional adverb as the subject slot and the verb findet in position II.

exercises.english: The neighbours are so noisy that we cannot sleep.
exercises.german: Die Nachbarn sind so laut, wir können nicht schlafen.
exercises.why: The negated infinitive closes the clause, and the modal können in position II expresses the blocked result.

exercises.english: The children were so excited that they shouted the whole way.
exercises.german: Die Kinder waren so aufgeregt, sie schrien den ganzen Weg über.
exercises.why: A degree adjective plus a following main clause: the subject sie comes after the connective and schrien is the finite verb in position II.

exercises.english: The lift is so slow that I take the stairs.
exercises.german: Der Aufzug ist so langsam, ich nehme die Treppe.
exercises.why: The second main clause contrasts two means of transport, with nimmt in position II and the preposition nehemen taking an accusative object.

exercises.english: The coffee is so bitter that I always add milk.
exercises.german: Der Kaffee ist so bitter, ich trinke ihn immer mit Milch.
exercises.why: The degree of bitter is followed by a compensating action; the accusative pronoun ihn is the object of trinke in position II.

exercises.english: The lecture was so boring that half the room fell asleep.
exercises.german: Die Vorlesung war so langweilig, die halbe Aula schlief ein.
exercises.why: A fronted quantifier die halbe Aula comes before the position-II verb schlief, and the separable verb closes the clause as ein.

exercises.english: The car is so old that it barely starts in winter.
exercises.german: Der Wagen ist so alt, er startet im Winter kaum noch.
exercises.why: A degree statement plus a result clause with a concessive negation: startet stands in position II and the negation kaum noch stays with the verb.

exercises.english: The soup smells so good that everyone wants some.
exercises.german: Die Suppe riecht so gut, jeder will davon haben.
exercises.why: so intensifies the degree of the verb riecht, and the result clause has the subject jeder in position I with will in position II.

exercises.english: Her replies are so short that nobody can tell what she means.
exercises.german: Ihre Antworten sind so kurz, man versteht nicht, was sie meint.
exercises.why: so modifies the degree of kurz, and the result clause contains a dass-clause inside which the verb meint comes last.

exercises.english: The rain was so heavy that the cellar flooded.
exercises.german: Der Regen war so stark, die Kellerräume wurden überflutet.
exercises.why: A degree clause and a passive result clause: the auxiliary wurde is in position II and the participle überflutet stands at the end.

exercises.english: The bread is so stale that nobody wants to buy it.
exercises.german: Das Brot ist so alt, niemand will es kaufen.
exercises.why: The modal will in position II expresses the refusal-like result, and the accusative pronoun es follows it as the object of kaufen.

exercises.english: It was so cold that we stayed indoors.
exercises.german: Es war so kalt, dass wir drinnen geblieben sind.
exercises.why: so plus the degree word kalt in the main clause, and the dass-clause closes with the perfect auxiliary hat replaced by sind and the participle at the very end.

exercises.english: The music was so loud that the neighbours complained.
exercises.german: Die Musik war so laut, dass sich die Nachbarn beschwert haben.
exercises.why: The verb of the dass-clause must be last; here the reflexive sich stands after the subject and haben with the participle beschwert ends the sentence.

exercises.english: I repeat, the deadline has been moved.
exercises.german: Sodass alle mich verstehen, wiederhole ich: Die Frist wurde verschoben.
exercises.why: Sodass can open the sentence; the dass-clause comes first with the verb verstehen last, and the main clause keeps its normal order with ich in position III.

exercises.english: She spoke so quietly that nobody heard her.
exercises.german: Sie hat so leise gesprochen, dass niemand sie gehört hat.
exercises.why: The degree is built with so plus an adverb after the auxiliary hat, and the dass-clause ends in a perfect with the participle gehört.

exercises.english: He is so punctual that everyone can rely on him.
exercises.german: Er ist so pünktlich, dass sich alle auf ihn verlassen können.
exercises.why: A modal verb closes the dass-clause: the conjugated können stands last after the object, which is the decisive position-II rule here.

exercises.english: So that costs are not overrun, we are meeting only online.
exercises.german: Sodass die Kosten nicht überschritten werden, treffen wir uns nur online.
exercises.why: A fronted sodass-clause with a passive verb: the auxiliary wird stands last, while the main clause keeps treffen in position II.

exercises.english: The file was so large that it could not be sent by email.
exercises.german: Die Datei war so groß, dass sie nicht per E-Mail verschickt werden konnte.
exercises.why: A passive inside the dass-clause: the modal konnte comes last, and the long participle attribute per E-Mail precedes it.

exercises.english: The child was so tired that it fell asleep in the car seat.
exercises.german: Das Kind war so müde, dass es auf dem Kindersitz einschlief.
exercises.why: The simple past subordinate clause is a common narrative choice, and the verb einschlief stands last after the prepositional phrase.

exercises.english: So that nobody is disturbed, please switch off your phone.
exercises.german: Sodass niemand gestört wird, schalten Sie bitte Ihr Handy aus.
exercises.why: The sodass-clause comes first with the passive auxiliary wird last, and the main clause inverts the pronoun to Ihr after schalten.

exercises.english: The prices are so high that we eat out less often.
exercises.german: Die Preise sind so hoch, dass wir seltener essen gehen.
exercises.why: The dass-clause ends with the separable verb gehen after its prefix ge-, while the main-clause subject is simply das Preise.

exercises.english: His application was so incomplete that it was rejected.
exercises.german: Sein Antrag war so unvollständig, dass er abgelehnt wurde.
exercises.why: A passive result clause where the auxiliary wurde occupies position II and the participle abgelehnt closes the dass-clause.

exercises.english: The road was so icy that everybody drove slowly.
exercises.german: Die Straße war so vereist, dass alle langsam gefahren sind.
exercises.why: The subject alle comes first inside the dass-clause, and the perfect verb gefahren sind must stand at the end as the final element.

exercises.english: It was so hot that we cancelled the meeting.
exercises.german: Es war so heiß, dass wir die Besprechung abgesagt haben.
exercises.why: The dass-clause stands first inside the subordinate, and the separable verb abgesagt haben is placed as a block at the end.

exercises.english: So that your application is accepted, you need the original certificate.
exercises.german: Sodass Ihr Antrag angenommen wird, brauchen Sie das Originalzertifikat.
exercises.why: A modal verb in the main clause: brauchen stands in position II, while the passive of the sodass-clause ends with wird.

exercises.english: The lecture was so long that two people fell asleep.
exercises.german: Der Vortrag war so lang, dass zwei Leute eingeschlafen sind.
exercises.why: The indefinite quantifier zwei Leute heads the dass-clause, and the perfect verb eingeschlafen sind closes it.

exercises.english: So that the plants do not dry out, we water them twice a day.
exercises.german: Sodass die Pflanzen nicht austrocknen, gießen wir sie zweimal am Tag.
exercises.why: The negated subordinate verb austrocknen is the last word of the fronted clause, and gießen is the position-II verb of the main clause.

exercises.english: The colours are so bright that you can see them from far away.
exercises.german: Die Farben sind so hell, dass man sie von weit her sieht.
exercises.why: The impersonal man is the subject of the dass-clause and the simple present sieht is the last element, as required.

exercises.english: The queue was so long that we only got tickets an hour before the start.
exercises.german: Die Schlange war so lang, dass wir erst eine Stunde vor Beginn Karten bekommen haben.
exercises.why: The perfect bekommen haben stands last; the time phrase is embedded in the subordinate clause before the subject and the verb.

exercises.english: He is so absent-minded that he always forgets his keys.
exercises.german: Er ist so zerstreut, dass er seine Schlüssel immer vergisst.
exercises.why: A repeated present subordinate clause; vergisst must be last, so the object seine Schlüssel and the temporal adverb immer come first.

exercises.english: The instructions were so unclear that nobody could follow them.
exercises.german: Die Anleitung war so unklar, dass niemand sie befolgen konnte.
exercises.why: The accusative pronoun sie stands after the subject, and the modal konnte is the last word of the dass-clause.

exercises.english: You improve fastest by speaking every day.
exercises.german: Du wirst am schnellsten besser, indem du jeden Tag sprichst.
exercises.why: indem expresses the means: the means is a full finite clause whose verb sprichst must stand last.

exercises.english: You save time by cooking once a week.
exercises.german: Du sparst Zeit, indem du einmal pro Woche kochst.
exercises.why: indem is a means-conjunction, and because its clause is finite the verb kochst must go last.

exercises.english: I found the flat by reading the ads every day.
exercises.german: Ich habe die Wohnung gefunden, indem ich jeden Tag Anzeigen gelesen habe.
exercises.why: A perfect clause after indem: the subordinate auxiliary habe is in position III and the participle gelesen closes the clause.

exercises.english: She kept quiet while I was speaking.
exercises.german: Sie schwieg, während ich sprach.
exercises.why: während here is modal in the sense of while and not, both verbs sit at the ends of their clauses: schwieg and sprach.

exercises.english: You cannot relax while you are still working.
exercises.german: Du kannst dich nicht entspannen, während du noch arbeitest.
exercises.why: A modal cannot as the main-clause verb: kannst is in position II, and the subordinate verb arbeitest comes last.

exercises.english: He earned the position by always being reliable.
exercises.german: Er hat die Stelle bekommen, indem er immer zuverlässig war.
exercises.why: indem states the means that led to the result, and the subordinate clause was stays in its position before the end.

exercises.english: You learn most when you make mistakes.
exercises.german: Du lernst am meisten, indem du Fehler machst.
exercises.why: The comparative am meisten frames the means clause, and machst is the last word of the indem-clause.

exercises.english: We heard strange noises while we were packing.
exercises.german: Wir haben seltsame Geräusche gehört, während wir die Koffer packten.
exercises.why: während introduces a simultaneous action; in the subordinate clause the subject wir comes first and packten is last.

exercises.english: You catch a cold by never airing the room.
exercises.german: Du holst dir einen Schnupfen, indem du bei jedem Bad lüftest.
exercises.why: indem names the means of catching a cold, and the subordinate clause is a full finite clause with the verb lüftest in the last position.

exercises.english: She finished the report by working late every evening.
exercises.german: Sie hat den Bericht fertiggestellt, indem sie jeden Abend länger arbeitete.
exercises.why: A perfect of the report with the participle placed before the connector, and the subordinate clause ends with arbeitete.

exercises.english: You spend much less if you book in early December.
exercises.german: Während du im Dezember buchst, zahlst du deutlich weniger.
exercises.why: während sets a contrast between the booking date and the price: the subordinate verb buchst is last, and zahlst stands in position II in the main clause.

exercises.english: He kept typing while the meeting was already over.
exercises.german: Er tippte weiter, während die Besprechung längst vorbei war.
exercises.why: während with two past clauses: the subordinate verb war stands last after the adverbial phrase.

exercises.english: You stay informed by reading the newspaper.
exercises.german: Du bleibst informiert, indem du die Zeitung liest.
exercises.why: indem plus a present clause; the pronoun du comes right after the connector and liest closes the clause.

exercises.english: The infant slept through the whole concert.
exercises.german: Das Baby schlief durch das ganze Konzert, während es von niemandem geweckt wurde.
exercises.why: während marks a simultaneous action that should have interrupted the situation: the passive subordinate verb wurde stands last.

exercises.english: He calmed down after drinking a glass of water.
exercises.german: Er beruhigte sich, indem er ein Glas Wasser trank.
exercises.why: A means-clause in the simple past; both trank and the preceding subject er follow the position-II rule for ihre finite verb.

exercises.english: Nobody noticed the error while the invoice was being checked.
exercises.german: Niemand bemerkte den Fehler, während die Rechnung geprüft wurde.
exercises.why: während with a passive clause: the subordinate verb wurde stands last after the participle attribute.

exercises.english: You reduce daily strain by taking short breaks.
exercises.german: Du baust jeden Tag Stress ab, indem du kurze Pausen machst.
exercises.why: The separable verb abbauen is split around the subject, and the means clause after indem ends with the conjugated verb machst.

exercises.english: She translated the letter although she should really have answered it.
exercises.german: Sie übersetzte den Brief, während sie ihn eigentlich hätte beantworten sollen.
exercises.why: während introduces a modal contrast: the main-clause verb steht in position II, and inside the subordinate clause the modal hätte and the infinitive sollen close it.

exercises.english: We heated up while the train was delayed.
exercises.german: Wir haben uns aufgewärmt, während der Zug Verspätung hatte.
exercises.why: während with a perfect in the main clause and a simple clause in the subordinate, where hatte comes last.

exercises.english: He mastered the language by watching films every day.
exercises.german: Er hat die Sprache beherrscht, indem er jeden Tag Filme schaute.
exercises.why: The perfect of the main verb is completed with beherrscht, and the means clause keeps its finite verb schaute in the final slot.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: This is the sponge with which you should clean the stove.
exercises.german: Das ist der Schwamm, womit du den Herd putzen solltest.
exercises.why: womit is a relative clause in the dative case after das, and the modal solltest is the last word of the clause.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: Do you have a pen with which I can sign the contract?
exercises.german: Hast du einen Stift, womit ich den Vertrag unterschreiben kann?
exercises.why: womit with a modal clause: kann comes last, and the case of the relative pronoun is determined by mit, i.e. dative.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: The kit is for repairing punctures on the road.
exercises.german: Das Set ist dafür da, wozu man Reifenpannen unterwegs reparieren kann.
exercises.why: wozu plus a modal clause answers the purpose question, and the modal kann is the last word of the subordinate clause.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: I am looking for a folder in which to keep the receipts.
exercises.german: Ich suche einen Ordner, wozu ich die Belege aufbewahre.
exercises.why: wozu is a purpose relative with zu plus an infinitive; the subject of the subordinate clause follows the connector.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: He is the neighbour whom I called at two in the morning.
exercises.german: Das ist der Nachbar, wozu ich um zwei Uhr geklingelt habe.
exercises.why: wozu-clause with a perfect: the preposition zu plus dem means for what, and habe plus the participle geklingelt is the closing block.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: This is the room in which we keep the receipts.
exercises.german: Das ist der Raum, wozu wir die Belege legen.
exercises.why: A wozu relative clause states the purpose of the room, and legen is the last word of the clause after the subject wir.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: This is the tool with which I tightened the screw.
exercises.german: Das ist das Werkzeug, womit ich die Schraube angezogen habe.
exercises.why: A womit-clause with a perfect: habe is in position III and the participle angezogen stands last.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: I need a tool we can use to avoid the traffic jam.
exercises.german: Ich brauche ein Werkzeug, womit wir den Stau umgehen können.
exercises.why: womit introduces the means of avoiding the jam, and the modal können is the last element of the relative clause.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: Why do you take two umbrellas?
exercises.german: Wozu brauchst du zwei Schirme?
exercises.why: wozu asks for a purpose and is answered with an infinitive, not with a prepositional phrase, so the verb brauchst keeps position II.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: What are you taking all these boxes for?
exercises.german: Wozu nimmst du all diese Kisten mit?
exercises.why: wozu expresses the purpose of a mitnehmen action, and the separable prefix mit- stands in position II before the verb stem nimmst.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: While his brother earns well, he barely gets by.
exercises.german: Während sein Bruder gut verdient, kommt er kaum über die Runden.
exercises.why: A concessive contrast: while the two states are simultaneous, the clause order is verb-final with kommt, and über die Runden is separable.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: While the company is growing, our department is shrinking.
exercises.german: Während die Firma wächst, schrumpft unsere Abteilung.
exercises.why: während contrasts two simultaneous developments; in the subordinate clause the verb wächst is last and in the main clause schrumpft holds position II.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: Although he is very rich, he lives modestly.
exercises.german: Während er sehr reich ist, lebt er bescheiden.
exercises.why: A clear modal contrast with während: the wealth and the modest lifestyle are held apart by the finite verb ist in the clause-final position.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: He talks big while he has achieved nothing.
exercises.german: Er prahlt viel, während er nichts erreicht hat.
exercises.why: während sets a lasting contrast against a perfect clause, whose participle erreicht hat is the closing block of the sentence.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: While the others were worried, she stayed calm.
exercises.german: Während die anderen besorgt waren, blieb sie ruhig.
exercises.why: A past-tense contrast with während: both clauses follow the verb-final rule, waren ends the first and blieb is in position II in the second.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: She claims she has no idea what she is doing, yet she finishes the course.
exercises.german: Während sie behauptet, keine Ahnung zu haben, schließt sie den Kurs ab.
exercises.why: A modal contrast built with während plus a nominalised infinitive: no idea zu haben is the compact nominal, and schließt is in position II.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: While the flats are getting more expensive, wages are hardly rising.
exercises.german: Während die Wohnungen teurer werden, steigen die Löhne kaum.
exercises.why: während presents a parallel development with an opposing tendency, and the subordinate verb werden comes last.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: The teacher explained the rule with a few clear examples.
exercises.german: Ich brauche ein Werkzeug, womit ich die alte Farbe entfernen kann.
exercises.why: womit-clause in the dative with the modal kann last; it names the instrument with which the paint can be removed.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: While we were waiting, a colleague came by with the missing file.
exercises.german: Während wir warteten, kam eine Kollegin mit der fehlenden Datei vorbei.
exercises.why: während is temporal here, not modal: the two past actions run in parallel, with kam in position II and vorbei closing the separable verb.

exercises.skill: Modal connectors: womit / wozu, and während contrast
exercises.english: He showed us the app with which he plans his trips.
exercises.german: Er zeigte uns die App, womit er seine Reisen plant.
exercises.why: A womit-clause in the dative after die App; in the subordinate clause the subject er follows the connector and the verb plant is last.
